passage:
Monday: Vishal stared at the police officer waving cars through the junction. "Is he scary, Mummy?"
"No, beta. Police are helpers. If you are ever lost, go to them," said Usha.
Thursday: At the bus stand Vishal waved at another officer, who waved back. "He has a shiny whistle," he told Usha.
Saturday: At the fair, Vishal let go of Usha's dupatta to look at a balloon and lost her in the crowd. His chin wobbled, but he walked to the officer near the gate. "I am Vishal. I lost Mummy." The officer knelt down and lifted a radio.

qa.q: Where did Vishal go when he lost Usha at the fair?
qa.a: He walked to the officer near the gate.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling on Monday when he stared at the officer?
qa.a: He was curious and unsure whether the officer was kind or scary, which is why he asked Usha.

qa.q: What made it easier for Vishal to act when he was lost?
qa.a: Usha had told him that police are helpers, and he had seen an officer wave back, so he knew whom to approach.

qa.q: What would change if Usha had said the police would take him away when he was naughty?
qa.a: Vishal would probably fear officers and might hide from them instead of asking for help when he was lost.

grounding: A child wonders whether police are kind or scary, is taught they are helpers, and goes to one when lost.

passage:
"Darshan, go on, give Madhav Uncle a kiss. He came all this way," said Mummy.
"Come here, champ, one kiss!" Madhav said, bending down with open arms.
Darshan hid behind Mummy's legs. "No."
"Darshan, be polite," Mummy began, then looked at his face and paused. "Beta, does it feel yucky?"
He nodded.
"Then you do not have to. Would you like to wave or give a high five?"
He held out his palm. Madhav laughed and tapped it lightly. "High five it is!"
"Your body is yours," Mummy whispered.

qa.q: What did Darshan offer Madhav in the end?
qa.a: He offered a high five.

qa.q: How does Darshan feel about giving the kiss?
qa.a: He is uncomfortable: he hides behind Mummy's legs, says no, and nods when she asks if it feels yucky.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that respected Darshan's no?
qa.a: She looked at his face, changed her mind, offered a wave or a high five, and told him his body is his own. 🤍

qa.q: How might Madhav see Darshan's refusal?
qa.a: He seems to take it in good part, since he laughs and accepts the high five; to him the kiss was probably meant as friendly.

grounding: A child is told to kiss a visiting uncle, feels uncomfortable, and the parent changes course and respects the no.

passage:
In the preschool story corner, Anand's class was talking about secrets. Tarun's hand shot up.
"I tell Mummy everything. Even secrets."
"Even secrets?" Anand asked.
"Yes. Last week a big boy on the van said, don't tell. I told Mummy anyway. She says no grown-up or big kid should ask me to keep a secret from her. I feel safe when I tell."
"What do you do if someone says don't tell?"
"I run and tell Mummy!"
Anand smiled. "Tarun's Mummy taught him something very wise."
After circle, Anand sat with Tarun, heard about the big boy, said it was not Tarun's fault and told the head teacher that day.

qa.q: Who did Tarun tell about the big boy on the van?
qa.a: He told Mummy.

qa.q: How does Tarun feel about telling Mummy his secrets?
qa.a: He feels safe: he says so himself, and he is sure enough to tell her anyway when a big boy asks him not to.

qa.q: What could Anand do next to support the class?
qa.a: Anand could invite every child to name a trusted grown-up they would tell, and repeat that nobody should ask them to keep a secret from those grown-ups. 🙂

qa.q: How might Anand see Tarun's answer?
qa.a: Anand seems pleased, calling it wise, because a child who tells is protected and the other children hear it from a classmate.

grounding: A child knows he can tell his parent anything, including a secret someone asked him to keep, and feels safe.

passage:
Tariq stayed quiet in the car home from his cousin's flat. A grown-up there had touched him in a way that felt wrong and said, "Don't tell." His stomach hurt and he could not work out why he felt so scared. At home he tried to tell Dad, but Dad was on a work call and said, "Later, buddy."
Next morning he found his teacher, Liam, and whispered, "Someone said not to tell."
Liam knelt down and listened without hurrying. "Thank you for telling me. It is never your fault. I will stay with you, and we will go to the head teacher together, right now."

qa.q: Who did Tariq try to tell first when he got home?
qa.a: He tried to tell Dad.

qa.q: How did Tariq feel after the grown-up said don't tell?
qa.a: He was frightened and confused: his stomach hurt and he could not work out why he felt so scared.

qa.q: What did Liam do that helped Tariq?
qa.a: Liam knelt down, listened without hurrying, said it is never Tariq's fault, stayed with him and took him to the head teacher straight away. 🤍

qa.q: What might it have been like for Tariq when Dad said later?
qa.a: He may have felt he could not get the words out or that no one would listen, yet he kept trying with another grown-up the next day.

grounding: A child touched wrongly and told not to tell feels frightened and confused; he keeps telling until a trusted grown-up helps.

passage:
"Hold my hand, Karthik. Look, the light is red."
"Red means stop!"
"That's right, even for us," said Sabina, halting at the kerb. "Cars are big and cannot stop quickly."
"Why are you waiting, Mummy?"
"Because I follow the rule too."
A man hurried across in front of them. "He did not wait!" Karthik said.
"No. We wait, because the rule keeps us safe."
The little green man lit up. "Now?"
"Look left, look right first."
They crossed together, and Karthik puffed out his chest. "I stopped at the red!"

qa.q: What did Karthik say red means?
qa.a: He said red means stop.

qa.q: How does Karthik feel after crossing?
qa.a: He feels proud: he puffs out his chest and announces that he stopped at the red.

qa.q: What helped Karthik understand the rule?
qa.a: Sabina explained in simple words that cars cannot stop quickly and followed the rule herself even when someone else did not.

qa.q: What would Karthik see if Sabina had crossed against the light with the man?
qa.a: He would see that the rule is optional for grown-ups and might copy it, so her waiting shows him the rule matters.

grounding: A child holds a parent's hand at a red light, feels proud following the rule, and the parent explains simply and models it.

passage:
"Nour, stop. Not the wall," said Selin, catching her sleeve as Nour put one foot on the garden wall.
Nour scowled and stamped. "I can climb!"
"That wall is too high and the ground is hard. That is a no. But the log pile is a yes. Want to climb there?"
Later, in the kitchen, Nour reached for the steaming pot.
"Hot! Hands back," Selin said, blocking her, and then handed over a wooden spoon and a bowl of dry beans to stir.
Nour, still a little cross, stirred hard and grinned as the beans clattered.

qa.q: What did Selin offer Nour to climb instead of the wall?
qa.a: Selin offered the log pile.

qa.q: What might Nour be feeling when she scowls and stamps?
qa.a: She seems frustrated and cross, because she wants to climb and does not think the wall is dangerous.

qa.q: How did Selin make the limit easier to accept?
qa.a: Selin said no clearly, gave a reason, and offered something safe to do straight away, such as a log pile and a bowl of beans.

qa.q: How might Selin see Nour's wish to climb and reach?
qa.a: Selin seems to see it as normal strong curiosity that needs firm limits and safe outlets, not as naughtiness.

grounding: A child wants to climb the wall and touch the hot pot; the adult sets firm limits and offers safe ways to explore.

passage:
In Pallavi's preschool class, the mats became a make-believe fair.
"Oh no, Himani is lost!" Pallavi said in a silly voice, and the children giggled.
Himani stood tall. "My name is Himani." She sang her Papa's phone number to the tune they had practised.
"Who can you ask for help?"
"A helper with a badge. Or a mummy with kids," said Himani, pointing at a toy police officer and a doll holding a baby.
"Wonderful," Pallavi said, clapping.
Himani grinned and asked for another turn, this time as the shopkeeper.

qa.q: What did Himani do with her Papa's phone number?
qa.a: She sang it to the tune they had practised.

qa.q: How does Himani feel about being lost in the game?
qa.a: She feels prepared and confident: she stands tall, answers easily, and asks for another turn.

qa.q: Why might practising as play work well for young children?
qa.a: It lets them rehearse the steps without fear, so they feel confident and can remember them when it matters. 🙂

qa.q: How might Pallavi see the game?
qa.a: Pallavi seems to see it as a fun way to build safety habits, keeping it silly and clapping when Himani answers.

grounding: A child who knows her name, her parent's number and whom to ask if lost feels prepared, having practised through play.

passage:
The corner shop was crowded, and Arnab was counting coins for the fruit when Gopika grabbed a plastic toy drum.
"Buy it, Papa, buy it!"
"Not today."
"Please, please!" Her voice went high and people turned to look.
Arnab crouched down. "Gopika, we have money for the fruit today. The drum costs more than we can spend now."
She wailed and flopped onto the floor. He stayed beside her, waited, and did not buy it.
"We will buy the mangoes, and you can carry the bag."
She hiccupped, took the bag in both arms, and sniffed all the way to the counter.

qa.q: What did Gopika grab in the shop?
qa.a: She grabbed a plastic toy drum.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when she flopped onto the floor?
qa.a: She was sad and frustrated because she wanted the drum and did not yet understand price.

qa.q: What went right in how Arnab handled the tantrum?
qa.a: He explained simply that the money was for the fruit, stayed beside her, and did not buy the drum, so crying did not pay.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel with people looking?
qa.a: He may feel a little uneasy, since the shop is crowded and he is short of money, yet he stays calm and keeps to his decision.

grounding: A child begs for a toy, the parent says no and explains money is for the fruit, and does not buy it to stop the tantrum.

passage:
"Ammi, can I pay?" Imran held a shiny coin tight.
"Yes. Give it to the shopkeeper and ask for the biscuits."
"Biscuits, please," said Imran, standing on tiptoe.
The shopkeeper put a small coin in his palm. "Your change."
"Why did he give me one back?"
"The biscuits cost less than your coin, so he returns the rest," said Parveen.
"Like magic!"
"Not magic. See, the coins have different numbers on them, so they buy different things."
He turned them over and over, then tucked the change in his pocket. "I am big now."

qa.q: What did Imran ask the shopkeeper for?
qa.a: He asked for the biscuits.

qa.q: How does Imran feel about paying by himself?
qa.a: He feels grown up: he says "I am big now" and holds the change proudly.

qa.q: How does Parveen help Imran understand money?
qa.a: She lets him try it himself and explains that things cost something and that coins have different numbers so they buy different things.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper see Imran's purchase?
qa.a: They probably see a small child proudly buying for the first time, since they hand over the change kindly and patiently.

grounding: A child hands over a coin, gets change, and feels grown up, while the parent lets him try and explains cost and coin values.

passage:
Every Sunday, Ada tipped her piggy bank onto the rug and counted the coins into little piles.
"Six," she whispered, touching each one.
Grandpa Yosef sat beside her with his tea. "Still want the red kite?"
"Yes. But it needs lots more."
"You could buy the small sticker book now."
Ada thought about it, then shook her head. "I will wait for the kite."
She slid the coins back into the pig one by one, sat up straight, and patted its round belly. "Two more Sundays," she said.

qa.q: How many coins did Ada count?
qa.a: She counted six.

qa.q: How does Ada feel about waiting for the kite?
qa.a: She feels proud and patient: she says she will wait and sits up straight while putting the coins away.

qa.q: What could Grandpa Yosef do next to encourage Ada?
qa.a: He could keep counting the coins with her each Sunday and celebrate when she reaches her goal, without buying it for her.

qa.q: How might Grandpa Yosef see Ada's choice?
qa.a: He seems to see a child learning that waiting brings more, since he offers the sticker book as an easy choice and lets her decide.

grounding: A child saves coins in a piggy bank, counts them, and proudly waits to buy something she wants, learning delayed reward.
